name: SIEM & Security Monitoring
description: Collecting, normalizing and correlating security logs in a SIEM to write detections and triage alerts.

questions.question: What is the primary function of a SIEM?
options: Blocking malicious packets at the network edge
Encrypting data stored in databases
Scanning hosts for missing patches
Collecting and correlating logs from many sources to detect and alert on security events
questions.explanation: A Security Information and Event Management system centralizes logs, normalizes them and applies correlation rules to raise alerts and support investigations.

questions.question: Which Windows Security Event ID records a failed logon attempt?
questions.explanation: 4625 is 'An account failed to log on'. 4624 is a successful logon, 4688 is process creation and 7045 is a new service installed.

questions.question: What does log normalization in a SIEM accomplish?
options: Mapping fields from different log sources into a common schema so they can be searched and correlated together
Deleting old logs to save storage
Encrypting logs in transit
Converting all timestamps to the local time zone of the analyst
questions.explanation: Normalization parses heterogeneous logs (firewall, Windows, web) into consistent fields like src_ip and user so rules work across sources.

questions.question: In alert triage, what is a false positive?
options: A real attack that generated no alert
A real attack that was correctly alerted on
An alert triggered by benign activity that is not actually malicious
An alert that was closed without review
questions.explanation: A false positive fires on legitimate activity. A real attack with no alert is a false negative.

questions.question: Which correlation logic best detects a likely successful password-guessing attack?
options: Any single failed logon for any account
Any successful logon during business hours
More than 5 process creation events on a server per day
Many failed logons (4625) from one source within a short window, followed by a successful logon (4624) from the same source
questions.explanation: Correlating a burst of failures with a subsequent success from the same source indicates the attacker likely guessed valid credentials.

questions.question: How is MITRE ATT&CK typically used in a security operations center?
options: As a scoring system to prioritize vulnerability patches
As a knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques used to map detections and find coverage gaps
As a log format that every SIEM must ingest
As a compliance standard that defines log retention periods
questions.explanation: ATT&CK catalogs real-world adversary behaviors; SOCs map their detection rules to techniques to see which behaviors they can and cannot detect.

practical.title: Write a brute-force detection rule
practical.instructions: Write a detection rule or query (Splunk SPL, KQL, Elastic, Sigma, or clear pseudo-logic) that alerts when a single source IP generates 10 or more failed Windows logons (Event ID 4625) within 5 minutes.
practical.expected_output: A query filtering EventCode/EventID 4625, grouping/counting by source IP (e.g. IpAddress/src_ip) over a 5-minute window, and alerting where count >= 10. Example SPL: index=wineventlog EventCode=4625 | bin _time span=5m | stats count by _time, src_ip | where count >= 10

rubric.description: Groups or counts by source IP
rubric.hint: Aggregate by the source IP field (e.g. src_ip or IpAddress).
Alert when the count is at least 10.
Limit the count to a 5-minute window (e.g. span=5m, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m), timeframe: 5m).

tasks.title: Understand log sources and key event IDs
tasks.description: Study the main log sources a SIEM ingests (Windows Security, Linux auth, firewall, web proxy) and list the most important Windows event IDs for authentication and process activity. Browse the related ATT&CK techniques.
tasks.completion_criteria: A reference sheet of at least 10 event IDs or log types with what each indicates and a related ATT&CK technique.

tasks.title: Complete a beginner SOC/SIEM lab
tasks.description: Work through an introductory SIEM or SOC analyst room on TryHackMe, running searches over sample logs to answer investigation questions.
tasks.completion_criteria: At least one SIEM-focused room completed with saved queries for each question.

tasks.title: Write and test Sigma detection rules
tasks.description: Read several community Sigma rules, then write three of your own for behaviors like brute force, new service installation and suspicious PowerShell. Test them against sample logs in a lab SIEM.
tasks.completion_criteria: Three valid Sigma rules, each mapped to an ATT&CK technique and shown firing on test data.

tasks.title: Build a home-lab SIEM with dashboards
tasks.description: Deploy a free SIEM (e.g. Splunk Free, Elastic or Wazuh) in a lab, forward logs from at least two machines you own, and build a dashboard plus alerts for authentication anomalies. Simulate benign test events to validate alerts and tune false positives.
tasks.completion_criteria: A working lab ingesting two or more sources, a dashboard, and at least three alerts with documented tuning decisions.
